BACKGROUND: Post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery (VO 2 Rec) is slow in advanced heart failure. We sought to establish easily derived VO 2 Rec measures and evaluate their cardiospecificity and prognostic relevance in patients with dyspnea on exertion. We further sought to determine VO 2 Rec modifiability proportional to changes in cardiac function with disease-specific treatment of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. METHODS: VO 2 Rec patterns were evaluated in relation to cardiac performance and the primary outcome of heart failure hospitalization or death in a referral cohort with dyspnea on exertion undergoing cardiopulmonary exercise testing with hemodynamic monitoring (MGH-ExS [Massachusetts General Hospital Exercise Study]). We then investigated longitudinal measures of VO 2 Rec in the pivotal phase 3 randomized controlled trial SEQUOIA-HCM (Safety, Efficacy, and Quantitative Understanding of Obstruction Impact of Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy) of aficamten versus placebo for 24 weeks in participants with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. For both cohorts, VO 2 Rec was uniformly measured as time for VO 2 to decline by >0%, 12.5% (VO 2 T 12.5% ), 25%, and 50% of peak VO 2 . RESULTS: Among 814 MGH-ExS patients (58±16 years of age, 58% women), those with a longer VO 2 T 12.5% (≥35 versus <35 seconds) demonstrated elevated exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure to cardiac output slope ( P <0.0001) with no difference in peripheral oxygen extraction ( P =0.11). For each 15-second increase in VO 2 T 12.5% , the hazard ratio for heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death was 1.54 (95% CI, 1.35–1.76; P <0.001). In SEQUOIA-HCM participants with cardiopulmonary exercise testing at baseline and week 24 (n=263, 59.1±2.9 years of age, 41% women), baseline VO 2 T 12.5% was 45±20 seconds and improved 8 seconds (95% CI, −12 to −5 seconds; P <0.001) with aficamten treatment compared with placebo at 24 weeks. Participants treated with aficamten versus placebo were more likely to improve VO 2 T 12.5% by ≥15 seconds (odds ratio [OR], 3.7 [95% CI, 1.9–6.9]; number needed to treat=4.8). Shortening of VO 2 T 12.5% correlated with reduced NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide), high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I, and left ventricular outflow tract gradient (all P <005). CONCLUSIONS: This study established VO 2 T 12.5% as a new measure that reflects cardiac performance during exercise and predicted heart failure event-free survival. Furthermore, VO 2 T 12.5% improved proportional to improvements in left ventricular outflow tract gradient and cardiac biomarkers in response to aficamten treatment, a cardiospecific therapy for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The simplicity and physiological relevance of VO 2 T 12.5% support its regular inclusion in cardiopulmonary exercise testing protocols evaluating cardiac function during exercise. This study reports multiple novel measures of oxygen uptake (VO 2 ) recovery after incremental exercise, highlighting that early VO2 recovery, measured as the time to recover 12.5% of peak VO2 (VO2T12.5%), is an easily derived measurement of metabolic resilience that closely reflects cardiac but not peripheral performance during exercise and predicts heart failure outcomes. In a separate clinical trial cohort from the SEQUOIA--HCM (Safety, Efficacy, and Quantitative Understanding of Obstruction Impact of Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy) trial, we demonstrated that VO2T12.5% improves proportionate to improvements in cardiac function in response to aficamten treatment, a myocardial disease–specific intervention in patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. What Are the Clinical Implications? Measurements of VO 2 recovery are not currently reported in cardiopulmonary exercise tests conducted in clinical practice or in clinical trials. VO 2 recovery assessment is noninvasive, simple to perform, and holds promise in helping to ascertain cardiospecific limitations to exercise capacity. VO2T12.5% complements other physiological measurements assessed during exercise and merits incorporation into cardiopulmonary exercise testing–based assessments of cardiac performance. VO2T12.5% deserves consideration as an important clinical trial end point when evaluating future cardiac interventions.

Impaired functional capacity is a cardinal manifestation of cardiovascular diseases, including heart failure (HF) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, even when euvolemic. However, functional capacity metrics in clinical practice and in clinical trials, such as New York Heart Association functional class, self-reported physical limitation, 6-minute walk distance, and peak oxygen uptake (VO 2 ), reflect composite inputs of multiple organ systems that collectively contribute to physical activity limitations. Even in advanced HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), careful invasive hemodynamic measurements during exercise have revealed significant interpatient heterogeneity related to whether central cardiac performance or peripheral O 2 use is predominantly impaired. 1 The patients with HFrEF and a predominant central cardiac limitation to exercise (55% of the study cohort) experienced a 5-fold greater risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes. 1 Hence, there is an unmet need to derive noninvasive exercise response patterns that specifically reflect cardiocentric exercise limitations. VO 2 recovery (VO 2 Rec) patterns capture the metabolic consequences of increasing metabolic rate during exercise, providing quantitative measurement of metabolic resilience. In patients with established severe HF, small studies by our group and others 2 , 3 have linked prolonged VO 2 Rec to worse cardiac output (CO) augmentation during exercise and to increased risk of adverse outcomes independent of peak VO 2 . However, it is unknown whether VO 2 Rec patterns specifically reflect cardiocentric deficits versus pulmonary or peripheral impairment or remain prognostic in heterogeneous cohorts of patients with dyspnea on exertion (DOE). In addition, it has not been determined whether VO 2 Rec is modifiable with interventions that directly augment cardiac performance in randomized controlled trials. The primary aims of this study were to: (1) establish novel and easily derived measurements of VO 2 Rec kinetics and report their values in a referral cohort of ambulatory patients with DOE; (2) relate VO 2 Rec to invasive hemodynamic, pulmonary, and peripheral O 2 extraction measurements during exercise; (3) determine the prognostic value of VO 2 Rec in the referral cohort; and (4) evaluate VO 2 Rec, defined by time for VO 2 to decline by >12.5% in a multicenter trial with repeated measurements of VO 2 T 12.5% . This cohort will be used to evaluate whether aficamten, a therapy known to be cardiospecific, is able to modify VO 2 T 12.5% in patients with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) enrolled in SEQUOIA-HCM (Safety, Efficacy, and Quantitative Understanding of Obstruction Impact of Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy; URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT05186818), a phase 3 randomized controlled trial of aficamten versus placebo. We hypothesized that VO 2 T 12.5% , a simple, single-threshold measurement of VO 2 Rec, provides a sensitive noninvasive surrogate for identifying impaired cardiac performance during exercise in a referral cohort with DOE. We further hypothesized that delayed VO 2 T 12.5% identifies patients at increased risk of HF hospitalization and all-cause death in the referral cohort. Finally, we hypothesized that, in a multicenter trial cohort, delayed VO 2 T 12.5% will be improved by aficamten, an effective cardiospecific treatment in SEQUOIA-HCM. METHODS Data Sharing The data supporting the findings of this study from the MGH-ExS (Massachusetts General Hospital Exercise Study) are available upon reasonable request. For data related to the SEQUOIA-HCM randomized controlled trial of aficamten versus placebo, qualified researchers may submit a request containing the research objectives, end points/outcomes of interest, statistical analysis plan, data requirements, publication plan, and qualifications of the researcher(s). Requests are reviewed by a committee of internal and external advisors. If approved, data necessary to address the research question will be provided under the terms of the data sharing agreement. Requests will be considered after applications for marketing authorization in the United States and Europe have been reviewed and final decisions rendered. Requests may be submitted to medicalaffairs@cytokinetics.com. Sample Population MGH-ExS, Referral Cohort The MGH-ExS cohort was defined with the intent to explore the relationship between VO 2 Rec and the primary outcome measure of HF hospitalization and all-cause death. The cohort was comprised of consecutive patients referred to a single tertiary care center from May 2011 to November 2022 for evaluation of DOE. Patients underwent a cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) with concurrent invasive exercise hemodynamic monitoring and had at least 3 minutes of measured post-exercise gas exchange data recorded. From this sample, we excluded patients who had a left ventricular ejection fraction <50%, previous lung or heart transplantation, severe valvular heart disease, known infiltrative or constrictive heart disease, or failure to achieve a respiratory exchange ratio >1.0 in the absence of peak heart rate (HR) >85% predicted (n=814; Figure S1 ). Only patients without missing data for VO 2 Rec measures were included, and missing data for covariates were considered missing at random. All patients provided written informed consent, and this study was approved by the Massachusetts General Brigham institutional review board. SEQUOIA-HCM, Clinical Trial Cohort The rationale for, and design of, SEQUOIA-HCM have been previously described. 4 , 5 In brief, this was a phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, multicenter trial (101 sites in 14 countries) in participants with oHCM with a primary end point of change in peak VO 2 at 24 weeks, adjudicated by the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) CPET Core Laboratory. Participants were recruited between February 1, 2022, and May 15, 2023. Each participant underwent measurement of cardiac biomarkers, including NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide) and hs-cTnI (high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I), CPET on a treadmill or cycle ergometer without invasive hemodynamic measurements, and rest and Valsalva echocardiography. Patients with a left ventricular outflow tract gradient (LVOT-G) ≥30 mm Hg when resting and ≥50 mm Hg after Valsalva, New York Heart Association functional class II to III symptoms, baseline peak VO 2 ≤90% of predicted, and respiratory exchange ratio ≥1.05 were eligible to participate. Individuals were excluded if they had a history of syncope or sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia with exercise within 6 months before screening or were unable to exercise on a treadmill or cycle. Aficamten doses were individualized to achieve the lowest effective dose resulting in a Valsalva LVOT-G <30 mm Hg while maintaining a left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50%. 6 Participants, investigators, and sponsors were masked to the echocardiograms and NT-proBNP levels. The trial was approved by the regulatory agencies in the participating countries and by the institutional review board or ethics committee at each trial center. This report adhered to the CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) reporting guidelines ( Supplemental Material ). Right Heart Catheterization and CPET MGH-ExS Methods used to perform the comprehensive CPET in this study have been previously described in detail. 7 Patients underwent placement of a pulmonary arterial catheter via the internal jugular vein and a systemic arterial catheter via the radial artery. Measurements of end-expiratory resting mean right atrial pressure, mean pulmonary arterial pressure, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) were obtained from participants in supine and upright positions (averaged across ≥3 respiratory cycles at rest and in the upright position during each minute of exercise). Fick CO was determined at the same intervals by measuring VO 2 and simultaneous radial arterial and mixed venous O 2 saturation (in conjunction with hemoglobin) to calculate the arteriovenous O 2 content difference (Ca-vO 2 ). Patients performed maximum incremental exercise using an upright cycle ergometer with an individualized ramp protocol (5 to 25 W/min) targeting 8 to 12 minutes of exercise, with breath-by-breath gas exchange variables measured using a Breezesuite metabolic cart (MedGraphics, Saint Paul, MN). After peak exercise was achieved, the ergometer resistance was removed, and patients were instructed to continue unloaded pedaling for 1 minute at 60 rpm, followed by 2 minutes of passive upright rest. Pulmonary arterial catheter pressure measurements and Fick CO were assessed 2 minutes after the cessation of loaded exercise. SEQUOIA-HCM The CPET Core Laboratory (MGH) designed the CPET protocol for SEQUOIA-HCM to closely mirror the protocol used at MGH that used the exercise methodology available at the site (cycle ergometer or treadmill, 45% and 55%, respectively). CPET was performed at baseline and week 24 using the same exercise modality. The MGH laboratory received raw breath-by-breath data from each participating site and interpreted CPETs in accordance with the CPET Core Laboratory manual of operations. Measurement of post-exercise VO 2 Rec patterns was prespecified as an exploratory end point. All CPET data were interpreted in a blinded manner. Measurement of VO 2 Kinetics The processing of the gas exchange data was performed identically to clinical tests in the MGH CPET clinical laboratory, using mid-5-of-7 processing of breath-by-breath data with an “inadequate breath filter” at a tidal volume of <50 mL within the Breezesuite software system commercially available with Medgraphics metabolic carts. In both study populations, VO 2 Rec was measured using 4 different time points, including time for VO 2 to decline by >0% (VO 2 T 0% ), VO 2 T 12.5% , 25% (VO 2 T 25% ), and 50% (VO 2 T 50% ), of which VO 2 T 0% and VO 2 T 50% have been previously described. 2 , 3 VO 2 T 12.5% and VO 2 T 25% were measured as the time for VO 2 to decline by12.5% and 25% of peak VO 2 after adjustment for individual resting VO 2 (Figure 1 ). Corresponding values were derived for the VO 2 component variable O 2 pulse (O 2 pulse = VO 2 /HR) at T 12.5% using its respective peak exercise and rest measurements. Peak HR was defined as the highest HR achieved during the exercise test. Peak VO 2 and peak O 2 pulse were defined as the highest 30-second median of O 2 uptake and O 2 pulse during the last 90 seconds of exercise. Percent predicted peak VO 2 was calculated using the formula derived by Hansen et al in MGH-ExS. 8 The Fletcher formula was originally applied to derive VO 2 % in SEQUOIA-HCM, 9 but the formula of Hansen et al was applied for this substudy to harmonize analyses with the MGH-ExS. The lowest (nadir) 30-second average ratio of minute ventilation (VE) to exhaled CO 2 defines the VE/VCO 2 nadir, and the slope of VE to VCO 2 defines the VE/VCO 2 slope. The VO 2 /work rate slope was calculated as the slope of VO 2 to external work beginning 60 seconds after initiation of the exercise ramp. Patient Subgroup Classification and Outcomes Assessment MGH-ExS Clinical characteristics and risk factor assessment, including NT-proBNP measurements, were obtained on the same day CPET was performed. Echocardiograms were preferentially acquired on the day of CPET, but to maximize data completeness, echocardiograms were permissible within 1 year of the study. Subgroups in MGH-ExS were created by using each participant’s hemodynamic profile, NT-proBNP level, left atrial size, and left ventricular mass ( Figure S1 ). Consistent with the recently advanced universal definition of HF, 10 participants were classified as meeting the diagnostic criteria for HF and had evidence of hemodynamic impairme

oups in MGH-ExS were created by using each participant’s hemodynamic profile, NT-proBNP level, left atrial size, and left ventricular mass ( Figure S1 ). Consistent with the recently advanced universal definition of HF, 10 participants were classified as meeting the diagnostic criteria for HF and had evidence of hemodynamic impairment (heart failure preserved ejection fraction-hemodynamic impairment [HFpEF-HDI]) if PCWP was elevated at rest or during exercise (supine PCWP ≥15 mm Hg or PCWP/CO slope ≥2.0 mm Hg/L per minute) with either elevated NT-proBNP (≥125 pg/mL) or an echocardiographic structural abnormality that included left atrial enlargement (>34 mL/m 2 ) 11 or left ventricular hypertrophy (>95 g/m 2 in women and >115 g/m 2 in men). 11 Filling pressures both at rest and during exercise were used, as they can independently identify patients with HF at risk of functional impairment and adverse outcomes. 12 , 13 In contrast, patients with normal PCWP at rest and a normal PCWP/CO slope during exercise were considered to have noncardiac dyspnea (NCD). Notably, those with elevated filling pressures who were missing additional diagnostic data (eg, NT-proBNP or an echocardiogram within 1 year) to corroborate the diagnosis of HFpEF were not included for between-group analyses; however, these patients were included in analyses of available measures of VO 2 Rec patterns. All available medical records were reviewed with the following clinical outcomes adjudicated by a panel of cardiologists through December 2023, including first HF hospitalization (defined as any hospitalization for principal HF cause) and all-cause mortality, which was ascertained using the Social Security Death Master File and electronic hospital records. Statistical Analysis MGH-ExS All statistical analyses were performed using R Studio (version 2023.06.1+524) on base R (version 4.3.1). Categorial data were compared using χ 2 test, and continuous data were compared using a t test. To evaluate the discriminatory performance of input variables, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was used (Figure 2 C), with the discriminative ability of a model assessed by calculating the area under the curve (AUC). The true positive rate (sensitivity) and false positive rate (1-sensitivity) were computed at varying classification thresholds. The AUC was reported as a measure of overall classification performance, where a value of 0.5 indicates no discrimination (random chance), and a value of 1.0 represents perfect classification. The ROC curve was visualized, and comparisons between ROC curves were performed using a DeLong test to assess statistical differences in AUC values. Values are reported as the AUC±SE of the model. To assess the relationships between VO 2 T 12.5% and other relevant variables, we used linear regression ( Figure S2 ), multivariable linear regression (Figure 2 D), and Spearman correlation ( Figure S3 ). Before linear, multivariable, and Cox regression, the skewness of the data was measured and formally tested using the Agostino test. Highly skewed data ( P >0.05) was log_e transformed. The ability of VO 2 T 12.5% to improve the variance explained in a model for cardiac performance (PCWP/CO slope) during exercise was evaluated by sequentially adding clinically relevant participant characteristics (age, sex, and body mass index [BMI]) in addition to CPET gas exchange measures previously established for clinical use in evaluation of patients with HF (percent predicted peak VO 2 , VO 2 /work slope, and VE/VCO 2 nadir) to a multivariable linear model for PCWP/CO slope before adding VO 2 T 12.5% . The values represented in Figure 2 D show the R 2 of the multivariable model. The likelihood ratio test was used to test whether each sequential measure in the model significantly improved the R 2 of the model. The relationship between VO 2 T 12.5% and the primary outcome measure of HF hospitalization and all-cause death was assessed using Cox regression with binned data and continuous data after standardization before and after adjustment for participant characteristics and commonly used medications with a plausible impact on exercise response patterns (beta-blockers and diuretics). The performance of the threshold of 35 seconds for prolonged VO 2 T 12.5% was visualized with Kaplan-Meier analysis (Figure 3 ), including other relevant clinical covariates commonly used in HF prognostication (NT-proBNP and percent predicted VO 2 ). SEQUOIA-HCM The full statistical analysis plan for CPET analyses was previously published. 5 , 14 Treatment effects were estimated using regression that included terms of treatment, randomization stratification factors (beta-blocker use status and CPET modality), and baseline value of the outcome. Additional analyses included a responder analysis for the proportional achievement of clinically meaningful thresholds for shifts in VO 2 T 12.5% (minimal [0 to <5 seconds], moderate [≥5 to <15 seconds], or large [≥15 seconds]) by treatment group and correlations between change in VO 2 T 12.5% with the change in other measures of treatment effect (symptoms, hemodynamics, and biomarkers) and evaluation of how change in VO 2 T 12.5% relates to change in other study-prescribed echocardiography and biomarker end points by correlation and multivariable regression analysis, allowing for potentially nonlinear relationships using restricted cubic splines with three knots. Missing VO 2 Rec end points at week 24, regardless of type of intercurrent events, were imputed using multiple imputation methodology under the missingness at random assumption because the proportion of patients with week 24 VO 2 Rec measures missing was expected to be very low. Statistical analyses were conducted using STATA (version 18, College Station, TX). All data are presented as number (percent), mean±SD, or median [interquartile range]. P values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

RESULTS Participant Characteristics Two cohorts were studied, a referral cohort from the MGH-ExS and a clinical trial cohort from the SEQUOIA-HCM trial. The baseline characteristics of the 814 participants in the MGH-ExS cohort are shown in Table 1 . The mean±SD age was 58±16 years, BMI was 29.5±6.5 kg/m 2 , 468 (58%) were women, and 56 (7%) were non-White. Patients had a high burden of cardiometabolic risk factors and comorbidities with a low exercise capacity (peak VO 2 was 16.5±5.6 mL/kg per minute, which was 74.8±18.7% of predicted). The SEQUOIA-HCM trial enrolled 282 participants with symptomatic oHCM; mean±SD age was 59±13 years, BMI was 28.1±3.7 kg/m 2 , 115 (41%) were women, and 21% were non-White (Table 1 ). Participants had a baseline peak VO 2 of 18.4±4.5 mL/kg per minute (79±18% predicted) in the aficamten group and 18.6±4.6 mL/kg per minute (81±20% predicted) in the placebo group, with no difference between the groups (Table 2 ). Patterns of VO 2 Rec and Their Relationships to Demographics and Exercise Measurements VO 2 Rec began immediately in 231 (48%) participants of the MGH-ExS cohort, resulting in VO 2 T 0% of 0 seconds with median values of 6 [interquartile range 0–19] seconds for the entire study population. Values of VO 2 T 0% frequently fell within the first few seconds after the initiation of recovery from incremental ramp exercise, prompting us to investigate early VO 2 Rec at prespecified thresholds beyond the initial delay period (12.5%, 25%, and 50% of the O 2 uptake recovery from peak VO 2 to resting VO 2 ; Figure 2 A). In the full MGH-ExS cohort, the initial mean±SD times for 12.5% and 25% of VO 2 Rec (VO 2 T 12.5% and VO 2 T 25% ) were 29±17 seconds and 44±18 seconds, whereas 50% of VO 2 Rec (VO 2 T 50% ) occurred at 74±23 seconds. There was no difference in VO 2 T 12.5% between sexes, with a mean±SD of 29.4±17.4 seconds for women and 29.0±17.9 seconds for men, with a t test P value of 0.71. We elected to focus on VO 2 T 12.5% for further analyses to capture early recovery kinetics without the same clustering of data around 0-second values, as is seen with VO 2 T 0% , while also being ascertainable within only 1 minute of recovery initiation in 94% of patients (versus 84% for VO 2 T 25% and 26% VO 2 T 50% ). Examination of component variables of VO 2 T 12.5% showed that VO 2 T 12.5% was closely related to O 2 pulse T 12.5% ( r 2 =0.48, P <0.001; Figure S2 ). In a multivariable logistic regression, individuals with longer VO 2 T 12.5% were more likely to be taking β-blockers ( P =0.003) and/or diuretics ( P =0.01) after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI. Calcium channel blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and angiotensin blockers did not relate to VO 2 T 12.5% after adjustment for demographics and other medication exposures. Spearman correlations between gas exchange measures (peak VO 2 , VE/VCO 2 nadir, and VO 2 T 12.5% ) and demographics and cardiac, pulmonary, and peripheral function are reported in Figure S3 . Compared with peak VO 2 , VO 2 T 12.5% was related to a greater degree to left atrial enlargement, rest and exercise PCWP, and pulmonary arterial pressure (all P≤ 0.01). In contrast, peak exercise pulmonary function as measured by physiologic dead space (dead space volume/tidal volume) related more closely to peak VO 2 (ρ=−0.39, P <0.001) and VE/VCO 2 (ρ=0.64, P <0.001) than VO 2 T 12.5% (ρ=0.28; both comparisons P <0.05), whereas percent predicted peak arteriovenous oxygen content difference (Ca-vO 2 divided by venous hemoglobin concentration) related only to peak VO 2 (ρ=0.20, P <0.001) and VE/VCO 2 (ρ=−0.09, P =0.02). Optimizing Identification of Cardiac Impairment with VO 2 T 12.5% We then assessed how well VO 2 T 12.5% discriminates impaired central cardiac function in HFpEF-HDI (n=228) from NCD (n=363). In ROC analysis, VO 2 T 12.5% showed improved differentiation of HFpEF-HDI and NCD compared with VO 2 T 0% (AUC 0.72 and 0.63, respectively; P <0.001) and similar discrimination to VO 2 T 25% and VO 2 T 50% (both AUC=0.75, P >0.05 compared with VO 2 T 12.5% ). In addition, VO 2 T 12.5% showed higher area under the curve (AUC) values than peak VO 2 % predicted, VE/VCO 2 nadir, and VO 2 /work slope in differentiating HFpEF-HDI from NCD with an optimal point of division at 35 seconds (Figure 2 C). VO 2 T 12.5% remained significant in discriminating between groups after adjusting for demographics and the other noninvasive CPET measures (adjusted AUC=0.67, P <0.001). VO 2 Components 2 Minutes After Exercise Individuals with VO 2 T 12.5% ≥35 seconds compared with <35 seconds demonstrated slower average CO recovery (13 versus 42%) 2 minutes after exercise ( P <0.001; Figure 3 A) but no difference in the rate of recovery for Ca-vO 2 (97 versus 101% recovery, P =0.37; Figure 3 B). Individuals with prolonged VO 2 T 12.5% had delayed recovery in directly measured Fick stroke volume (SV) 2 minutes after exercise relative to their peak value (0% recovery) compared with participants with less than 35-second VO 2 T 12.5% (57% recovery, between-group P <0.001). However, there was no difference in their HR recovery patterns (44 versus 41%, P =0.82). These differential patterns are summarized in Figures 3 C and 3 D. VO 2 T 12.5% Correlates With Invasive Exercise Hemodynamic Measurements Separation of the MGH cohort into groups according to duration of early VO 2 T 12.5% showed that patients with VO 2 T 12.5% beyond 35 seconds demonstrated an elevated PCWP/CO slope with no difference in Ca-vO 2 % predicted (Figure 2 A and 2 B). Patient demographics and each of the following CPET gas exchange measures (VO 2 % predicted, VO 2 /work relationship, VE/VCO 2 nadir, and VO 2 T 12.5% ) explained 23% of the variability in the PCWP/CO slope (Figure 2 D). Inclusion of VO 2 T 12.5% improved the total variability explained by the model to 27% for PCWP/CO (model P <0.001). Age, VO 2 /work slope, and VO 2 T 12.5% were independently significant in the model (all P <0.001). Prognostication of DOE We observed 144 events (87 HF hospitalizations and 57 deaths) over a median follow-up time of 3.9 [1.8–7.1] years. The hazard ratio per standard deviation change in VO 2 T 12.5% in a multivariable Cox regression model for HF hospitalization and all-cause death was 1.36 [1.15–1.61], accounting for patient age, sex, and BMI, which does not change significantly when adjusting for β-blocker and diuretic use (HR, 1.31 [1.11–1.56]) and similarly remains unchanged when separately adjusted for percent predicted peak VO 2 (HR, 1.32 [1.12–1.56]). Individuals with prolonged VO 2 T 12.5% (≥35 seconds) show increased hazard for adverse outcomes (hazard ratio, 2.52 [1.76–3.62]; Figure 4 A), which was only modestly attenuated after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI (hazard ratio, 1.76 [1.20–2.60]; P =0.003) and separately for percent predicted peak VO 2 (HR, 1.89 [1.29–2.77], P =0.001). Further, VO 2 T 12.5% ≥35 seconds predicted risk for adverse outcomes in both sexes with a HR of 2.07 [1.22–3.51] for women versus 3.13 [1.90–5.17] for men. For each 15-second increase in VO 2 T 12.5% , there was a corresponding incremental increase in the risk for HF hospitalization and all-cause death (hazard ratio, 1.54 [1.35–1.76]; P <0.001). The combination of peak VO 2 % <70% and VO 2 T 12.5% ≥35 seconds identified a group of patients with significantly increased risk for HF hospitalization and all-cause mortality relative to those with impaired peak VO 2 and a normal VO 2 T 12.5% (hazard ratio, 4.55 [2.87–7.21]; P <0.001; Figure 3 B). Similarly, adding the categorical assessment of VO 2 T 12.5% further delineated the risk of adverse outcomes among those with NT-proBNP >125 pg/mL, the cut point used in the universal definition of HF ( P =0.01; Figure 4 C). SEQUOIA-HCM Intervention Cohort With Repeated Measures of VO 2 Rec At baseline, recovery of 0%, 12.5%, 25%, and 50% of peak VO 2 took a median of 11 seconds [0–30] and a mean 45±20, 66±21, and 115±32 seconds, respectively, in the aficamten treatment arm, with no difference versus placebo. At 24 weeks, VO 2 T 12.5% improved by 8 seconds (95% CI, −12 to −5 seconds; P <0.001) in the aficamten group compared with the placebo group. Those treated with aficamten were more likely to improve VO 2 T 12.5% by ≥15 seconds (OR=3.6 [95% CI, 1.9–6.9]; number needed to treat=4.8) than those on placebo (Figure 5 A). Shortening of VO 2 T 12.5% correlated with reduced NT-proBNP, hs-cTnI, and LVOT-G (at rest and with Valsalva) (Figure 5 B through 5 E; all P ≤0.005). On average, a 15-second improvement in VO 2 T 12.5% was associated with a median 18% [8%–26%] reduction in NT-proBNP, an 5.1 [1.7–8.4] mm Hg reduction in resting LVOT-G, and a 6.0 [2.1–9.9] mm Hg reduction in LVOT-G on Valsalva.

DISCUSSION In this study, we describe a novel approach to assessing post-exercise VO 2 Rec in a referral cohort of patients with DOE and preserved ejection fraction and in SEQUIOA-HCM trial participants with symptomatic oHCM. The major findings of our study were as follows: (1) VO 2 Rec (VO 2 T 0% , VO 2 T 12.5% , VO 2 T 25% , and VO 2 T 50% ) can be easily and uniformly acquired when gas exchange measurements are extended for 3 minutes into recovery during CPET; (2) VO 2 T 12.5% closely tracked with invasively derived exercise hemodynamic indices of HF in dyspneic individuals and outperformed other noninvasive CPET measurements, including peak VO 2 % predicted, VO 2 /work slope, and VE/VCO 2 nadir, when identifying impaired cardiac performance in HFpEF; (3) dissection of VO 2 component variables during recovery revealed differential recovery kinetics with more rapid and uniform normalization of Ca-vO 2 compared with CO, providing mechanistic insight into the relative cardiospecificity of VO 2 T 12.5% ; (4) VO 2 T 12.5% ≥35 seconds predicted all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization and further risk-stratified individuals with impaired peak VO 2 or elevated NT-proBNP with underlying symptomatic HFpEF; and (5) VO 2 T 12.5% was modifiable in response to myocardium-specific treatment (aficamten) for oHCM. Notably, this is the first study to describe VO 2 T 12.5% and to show that VO 2 T 12.5% relates to exercise invasive hemodynamic measurements in a large cohort of ambulatory patients with suspected HFpEF. Also, it is the first study to identify that VO 2 T 12.5% is reduced proportionate to improvements in cardiac function and other important clinical measures in response to a cardiospecific intervention of cardiac myosin inhibition with aficamten in oHCM. Comparison With Previous Observations Previous studies of VO 2 Rec patterns have primarily focused on T 1/2 (ie, VO 2 T 50% ) in small cohorts. Patti et al 15 reported average (SD) T 1/2 (or VO 2 T 50% ) in healthy control participants of 58±13 seconds compared with 111±51 seconds in those with HFrEF. Cohen-Solal et al 3 reported a VO 2 T 50% of 93±20 seconds for 72 patients with HF. Similarly, a preliminary study from our laboratory 2 also measured VO 2 T 50% with values of 115±40 seconds in HFrEF and 102±21 seconds in HFpEF. Patients with DOE in our HFpEF-HDI (88±27 seconds) group and participants with oHCM in SEQUOIA-HCM (116±35 seconds) more closely resembled the group with established HF, whereas NCD (67±19 seconds) approximated controls reported by Patti et al 15 HFpEF-HDI participants demonstrate a faster median VO 2 T 50% than the patients with HF reported in Patti et al 15 and participants with oHCM in SEQUOIA-HCM, which may be attributable to a larger degree of cardiac impairment in HFrEF (left ventricular ejection fraction 36±10%) and oHCM than in those with HFpEF-HDI. 16 , 17 Before this study, little was known about early post-exercise O 2 recovery patterns at time intervals shorter than VO 2 T 50% . VO 2 T 25% and VO 2 T 12.5% had not been described, whereas VO 2 T 0% was characterized in a preliminary study by our group, describing an initial delay in VO 2 Rec immediately after the cessation of exercise (VO 2 Rec delay or VO 2 T 0% ), with median values of 25 seconds in both HFpEF and HFrEF. The differences in values of VO 2 T 0% between this study (median 6 seconds overall and a median of 10 seconds in HFpEF-HDI) and our previous work are likely attributable to our inclusion criteria. We purposefully included patients with a wide array of ambulatory disease severities, leading to a broad interquartile range of 31 seconds, whereas the previous study only measured VO 2 Rec in patients with severe HF. Optimizing Selection of VO 2 Rec Measurements Within our broadly inclusive cohort, it was common to observe near-immediate VO 2 Rec (ie, VO 2 T 0% =0–10 seconds). In contrast, the later time points of early VO 2 Rec (VO 2 T 12.5% and VO 2 T 25% ) uniformly yield nonzero values and better discriminate between the presence and absence of hemodynamic impairment. There does not appear to be any benefit of measuring beyond VO 2 T 12.5% , as there is no significant increase in diagnostic certainty based on comparison of ROC AUC values ( P >0.05 for VO 2 T 50% and VO 2 T 25% versus VO 2 T 12.5% ) beyond this point, and longer periods of gas exchange measurement after exercise are requisite to derive VO 2 T 25% and VO 2 T 50% . Prolonged VO 2 T 12.5% Relates to Elevated Filling Pressures and Identifies HFpEF Our group and others have previously shown that the PCWP/CO slope is a reliable integrated measurement of an impaired hemodynamic response to exercise in HF and that individuals with a PCWP/CO slope ≥2 mm Hg/L per minute are at increased risk of adverse outcomes. 12 Participants with prolonged VO 2 T 12.5% demonstrate increased filling pressures with more hemodynamic impairment the longer the VO 2 T 12.5% . Mechanisms of Prolonged VO 2 Rec Cohen-Solal et al described multiple VO 2 Rec kinetics patterns after exercise in patients with HF, including individuals who continue to increase their VO 2 , others who plateau, and some who “rebound,” for whom VO 2 rapidly decreases but subsequently returns

.5% demonstrate increased filling pressures with more hemodynamic impairment the longer the VO 2 T 12.5% . Mechanisms of Prolonged VO 2 Rec Cohen-Solal et al described multiple VO 2 Rec kinetics patterns after exercise in patients with HF, including individuals who continue to increase their VO 2 , others who plateau, and some who “rebound,” for whom VO 2 rapidly decreases but subsequently returns close to peak VO 2 . 18 This VO 2 rebound has been subsequently described with other cardiac impairments. 19 – 22 Cohen-Solal et al further speculated that inadequate CO during exercise governs prolongation of VO 2 T 50% after evaluating phosphocreatine recovery in the skeletal muscle of patients with HFrEF. Our findings extend those of Cohen-Solal et al and are aided by the availability of direct measurements of CO and CavO 2 during exercise and recovery. 3 Mechanistic studies attribute the rebound observed by Cohen Solal et al to an increase in SV during early post-exercise recovery because of a decrease in end-systolic volume without change in end-diastolic volume. 22 , 23 This pattern is linked to reduced afterload from peripheral vasodilation immediately after exercise at the same time when external work that incurred O 2 debt ceases. Our study extends these findings by showing that VO 2 T 12.5% corresponds closely with the duration of O 2 pulse recovery measured with a similar technique ( Figure S2 ). We also show that Ca-vO 2 , 1 of the 2 components of O 2 pulse, recovers more rapidly than CO after peak exercise (Figure 3 A and 3 B). In contrast, SV, the other component of O 2 pulse, remains higher 2 minutes after exercise than peak exercise in individuals with the most prolonged VO 2 T 12.5% . The components of VO 2 (Ca-vO 2 , HR, and SV) are 97%, 43%, and 22% recovered 2 minutes after exercise, respectively. This differs from exercise onset and maintenance, as Ca-vO, HR, and SV gradually ascend during incremental exercise, but Ca-vO 2 is 97% recovered by 2 minutes after exercise, indicative of a rapid early descent. This indicates that individual VO 2 components recover at different rates after peak exercise and that exercise recovery kinetics must be considered to be mechanistically distinct from exercise onset and maintenance. A fundamental limitation of noninvasive CPET is the inability to parse relative impairment in all 3 component variables (HR, SV, and Ca-vO 2 ) during maximum incremental exercise. The differential recovery kinetics of VO 2 component variables provides a potential window into the within-exercise SV constraint that is relieved immediately after exercise, thereby attenuating overall VO 2 Rec (Figure 3 C and 3 D). Although our study highlights distinct rates of recovery of CO and Ca-vO2 at 2 minutes of recovery (Figure 3 ), future studies are indicated to ascertain recovery patterns of Fick variables at additional proximal time points of recovery encompassing early VO 2 Rec variables. How Does VO 2 Rec Differ From HR Recovery? The most established measure of exercise recovery to date is HR recovery, measured as beats-per-minute difference from peak exercise. Patients with HFpEF demonstrate impaired HR recovery 24 ; however, the results of our study argue that measurement of VO 2 Rec provides independent insight into a patient’s hemodynamic status, as VO 2 T 12.5% time corresponded to a longer O 2 pulse recovery time. Also, tertiles of VO 2 T 12.5% show no difference in percentage of HR recovered by 2 minutes among the 3 groups. These findings imply that measurement of VO 2 T 12.5% should be performed in addition to HR recovery for a comprehensive CPET protocol. Is VO 2 T 12.5% Modifiable With Interventions That Improve Cardiac Performance? SEQUOIA-HCM recently demonstrated that aficamten improved exercise capacity (peak VO 2 ), quality of life, and echocardiography indices of obstruction and diastolic performance in patients with oHCM. SEQUOIA-HCM was identified as a trial well suited to further assess the conclusion drawn from the MGH-ExS referral cohort that VO 2 T 12.5% is specific for changes in cardiac function because aficamten directly targets myocyte contractility in oHCM without off-target neurohormonal mechanisms such as those seen in drugs like angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitors 25 and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. 26 Here, we report that the average relative magnitude of improvement in VO 2 T 12.5% was 18%, compared with the 9% improvement in peak VO 2 and 7% improvement in VE/VCO 2 slope. We also found that aficamten improved VO 2 T 12.5% proportionately to improvements in levels of NT-proBNP and troponin as well as degree of LVOT obstruction. These data support the findings in our study that prolonged VO 2 T 12.5% is specific to impaired cardiac performance and that VO 2 T 12.5% should be considered for inclusion in standard CPET protocols deployed to evaluate cardiac reserve capacity during exercise. Further, the number needed to treat <5 for 15-second improvement suggests that clinical events may be impacted (as in the MGH-ExS cohort, in which each 15-second increase in VO 2 T 12.5% was associated with a >50% increase in HF hospitalization or all-cause death), although this finding requires further investigation. In addition, VO 2 T 12.5% is a promising noninvasive measurement that could be used to define impaired cardiac performance in human cardiac drug development randomized controlled trials. Limitations This study has several limitations. First, NT-proBNP level and complete echocardiography measurements were not available for every patient, which may have limited our ability to capture all those with HFpEF-HDI in the overall MGH-ExS cohort. However, entry into the comparison group (NCD) required normal filling pressures that prevented wrongful categorization of patients with missing data to the NCD group. Second, measurement of Ca-vO 2 at 2 minutes after exercise was not uniformly available, as this approach was not historically part of our invasive exercise testing protocol. Third, there was no functional imaging or invasive hemodynamic measurements during exercise in the SEQUOIA-HCM study, which confined our analysis to relating VO 2 T 12.5% to resting and post-Valsalva assessments of cardiac performance. Direct comparison of VO 2 T 12.5% to assessments of cardiac performance during exercise in oHCM merits investigation in future studies. Further studies are warranted to compare VO 2 Rec variables that are readily derivable from noninvasive data to further evaluate relative clinical performance of VO 2 kinetic measures across broad patient populations. Conclusions This study is the first to establish VO 2 T 12.5% as a measurement of metabolic resilience that closely reflects cardiac but not peripheral performance and predicts HF outcomes. Furthermore, VO 2 T 12.5% improves in response to aficamten treatment, a myocardial disease–specific intervention in patients with oHCM. In light of the ease of measurement during noninvasive CPET, VO 2 T 12.5% merits incorporation into CPET-based assessments of cardiac performance during exercise and consideration as a trial end point when evaluating cardiac interventions.
